full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. MONICO BADILLO, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > B. Criminal Liability > 8. Circumstances Affecting Criminal Liability > d. Aggravating Circumstances
topics: Treachery: suddenness alone is not enough; deliberate adoption of the means must be shown
No treachery when no witness saw how the attack began
Mode of appeal when the CA downgrades murder to homicide
Positive identification vs. denial and alibi; delay in reporting
Damages in homicide (Jugueta); deletion of exemplary damages

doctrine:
**Treachery cannot be appreciated when no witness saw how the attack began.** There is treachery when (1) the means of execution gave the person attacked no opportunity to defend himself or retaliate, and (2) those means were deliberately or consciously adopted (*People v. Corpin*). A "sudden" and "unexpected" attack is not enough by itself: the prosecution must show that the offender purposely adopted that mode of attack to ensure its execution without risk to himself. Treachery must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, as conclusively as the killing itself. It cannot rest on conjecture, and when there is no precise evidence of how the attack commenced, the doubt is resolved in favor of the accused. Without treachery, the killing is homicide under Article 249 of the RPC. Reiterated.

Appeals in criminal cases to the Supreme Court are generally by petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 (Rule 122, Sec. 3(e)). A notice of appeal filed with the CA is the mode under Rule 124, Sec. 13(c). Where the CA downgraded murder to homicide and imposed *reclusion temporal*, the Court held that the accused's notice of appeal was the wrong remedy. It nonetheless treated the appeal as a Rule 45 petition in the interest of substantial justice. Even under Rule 45, an appeal in a criminal case throws the whole case open for review, because guilt is essentially a question of fact.

Also reiterated:
- The trial court's assessment of the witnesses' credibility is accorded great weight.
- Minor inconsistencies (where in the house the victim was stabbed, how many times) and a two-month delay in reporting the crime do not impair credibility.
- Denial and alibi cannot prevail over positive identification by credible witnesses with no ill motive. Alibi requires proof of physical impossibility and is weakened when corroborated only by relatives.
- For homicide, the Court awarded PHP 50,000 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and temperate damages (*People v. Jugueta*), deleted the exemplary damages, and sustained attorney's fees under Article 2208.
facts:
Monico Badillo was charged with murder, qualified by treachery and evident premeditation, for stabbing Joseph Olbes to death at about 7:12 p.m. on September 14, 2008 in Barangay San Juan, Irosin, Sorsogon.

Prosecution witness Salvador was fishing at a nearby creek when he heard a loud noise from the victim's house. He looked over the concrete fence into the lighted kitchen and saw Badillo stabbing the victim several times on the upper stomach; the victim escaped. Witness Jomel had passed Badillo at the victim's gate on his way to the store. Later, while smoking outside his house, he saw Badillo leaving the victim's house holding a blood-stained knife. The victim died the same day. His wife, Marilou, testified that she paid counsel PHP 20,000 plus PHP 1,000 per appearance. The eyewitnesses reported the crime about two months later.

Badillo claimed that on that evening he was at home in Batuan, Masbate attending to his sick daughter, and that he had left Irosin in 2006. His cousins Felipe and Emilio corroborated his alibi.

On July 7, 2017, the RTC convicted Badillo of murder. It appreciated treachery because the stabbing was sudden and the victim was unarmed, and imposed *reclusion perpetua* with damages, including PHP 30,000 exemplary damages and PHP 20,000 attorney's fees. On February 15, 2019, the CA found no evidence that Badillo deliberately adopted a mode of attack, downgraded the crime to homicide, and imposed an indeterminate penalty. Badillo filed a notice of appeal, and both parties adopted their CA briefs.
issues: Whether Badillo availed of the proper remedy in elevating the CA decision through a notice of appeal.
Whether the lower courts correctly gave credence to the prosecution witnesses and rejected Badillo's denial and alibi.
Whether treachery attended the killing so as to qualify it to murder.
Whether the penalty and the damages awarded were proper.
ruling:
**1. No, but the Court treated the appeal as a Rule 45 petition.** Criminal appeals to the Court are generally by petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 (Rule 122, Sec. 3(e)), with a notice of appeal filed with the CA used in cases under Rule 124, Sec. 13(c). The CA downgraded the conviction to homicide, which changed the penalty from *reclusion perpetua* to *reclusion temporal*. Badillo therefore "availed of the wrong remedy" when he filed a notice of appeal. In the interest of substantial justice, the Court treated it as a Rule 45 petition. Although Rule 45 is limited to questions of law, the finding of guilt in a criminal case is essentially a question of fact, and an appeal throws the whole case open for review.

**2. Yes.** No cogent reason existed to disturb the uniform findings that Salvador and Jomel were straightforward, credible and had no motive to testify falsely. Discrepancies on where in the house the victim was stabbed and how many times are collateral matters. They do not impair credibility when the witnesses are consistent on the principal occurrence and on the identity of the assailant. Jomel's conduct was not unusual: he saw Badillo twice, before and after he had dinner. There is no standard reaction to a startling event, and the natural reluctance of eyewitnesses to get involved is understandable; "a two-month delay is hardly an indicium of a concocted story." Badillo's denial was bare. His alibi failed because transportation between Batuan, Masbate and Irosin, Sorsogon was available, so physical impossibility was not shown. Corroboration by his cousins, who are not disinterested witnesses, carries little weight.

**3. No. The crime is homicide.** The RTC relied on the suddenness of the attack on an unarmed victim, but suddenness alone is not treachery; there must be proof that the offender purposely adopted the mode of attack. **None of the prosecution witnesses saw how the assault began.** Salvador saw only the stabbing itself, and Jomel saw Badillo only before and after. Treachery must be proved as conclusively as the killing itself. "Even where all indicia tend to support the conclusion that the attack was sudden and unexpected, yet no precise data on this point exists, treachery cannot be taken into account." The Court could not assume that the victim was caught unaware or had no chance to defend himself. The doubt was resolved in Badillo's favor.

**4. The penalty was affirmed, and the damages were modified.** The indeterminate penalty the CA imposed for homicide without modifying circumstances was within the range allowed by the Indeterminate Sentence Law. Applying *People v. Jugueta*, civil indemnity and moral damages were reduced to PHP 50,000 each. PHP 50,000 temperate damages was added under Article 2224, because the heirs undeniably incurred funeral and burial expenses though the amount was not proved. The PHP 30,000 exemplary damages was deleted: exemplary damages may be awarded even without an aggravating circumstance, but the Court saw no reason for them here. The PHP 20,000 attorney's fees was sustained under Article 2208 because the heirs incurred costs in prosecuting the case. All amounts earn 6% interest from finality.
disposition: The appeal was DISMISSED. The CA Decision of February 15, 2019 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 09885 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATIONS. Badillo was found GUILTY of homicide and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six years and one day of *prision mayor*, as minimum, to 14 years, eight months and one day of *reclusion temporal*, as maximum. He was ordered to pay the victim's heirs PHP 50,000 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and temperate damages, plus PHP 20,000 attorney's fees and costs of suit. The award of exemplary damages was DELETED. All damages earn 6% interest per annum from finality until full payment.

bar_questions.q: At about 8:00 p.m., Ramon heard shouting from his neighbor Victor's house. He looked through the window and saw Tomas stabbing Victor, who was unarmed, several times in the chest. Nobody saw how the encounter started. The trial court convicted Tomas of murder, appreciating treachery because the stabbing was sudden and Victor was unarmed. Is the conviction for murder correct?

alac.answer: No. Tomas is liable only for homicide because treachery was not proved.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article 14(16) of the RPC, treachery exists when (1) the means of execution gave the person attacked no opportunity to defend himself or retaliate, and (2) those means were deliberately or consciously adopted. A sudden attack is not enough. Treachery must be proved as conclusively as the killing itself, and it cannot be appreciated when there is no precise evidence of how the attack began. (People v. Badillo, G.R. No. 249832, November 13, 2024)
alac.application: Ramon saw only the stabbing in progress, not how it began. Nothing shows that Tomas consciously chose a mode of attack that denied Victor any chance to defend himself. That Victor was unarmed and the blows were sudden does not prove that the means were deliberately adopted. Any doubt on the existence of treachery is resolved in favor of the accused, so the killing is not qualified.
alac.conclusion: Tomas should be convicted of homicide under Article 249 of the RPC, not murder.

bar_questions.q: Change the facts. Ramon testified that he saw Tomas hide behind Victor's kitchen door for several minutes, waiting. When Victor walked in carrying a basin of water with both hands and with his back to the door, Tomas rushed out and stabbed him in the back several times, giving him no chance to turn around. Was the killing attended by treachery?

alac.answer: Yes. Treachery was proved, so the crime is murder.
alac.legal_basis: Treachery requires that (1) the means of execution gave the victim no opportunity to defend himself or retaliate, and (2) those means were deliberately or consciously adopted (Art. 14(16), RPC). It must be proved as conclusively as the killing itself, which requires evidence of how the attack began. (People v. Badillo, G.R. No. 249832, November 13, 2024)
alac.application: Unlike in Badillo, the witness saw the attack from its start. Tomas waited in hiding and struck from behind while Victor's hands were occupied and his back was turned, a means that gave Victor no opportunity to defend himself or retaliate. His waiting in ambush and his choice of that moment show that he deliberately adopted the means to ensure the killing without risk to himself.
alac.conclusion: The killing was qualified by treachery, and Tomas is liable for murder.

bar_questions.q: The RTC convicted Pedro of murder and sentenced him to reclusion perpetua. The CA found treachery unproven, convicted him of homicide, and imposed an indeterminate penalty with a maximum within reclusion temporal. To bring the case to the Supreme Court, Pedro filed a notice of appeal with the CA. (a) Did Pedro avail of the proper remedy? (b) May the Supreme Court review the factual findings on which his guilt rests?

alac.answer: (a) No. The proper remedy was a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45, although the Court may treat his notice of appeal as such a petition in the interest of substantial justice. (b) Yes. The Court may review the factual basis of his conviction.
alac.legal_basis: Appeals in criminal cases to the Supreme Court are generally by petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 (Rule 122, Sec. 3(e)). In People v. Badillo (G.R. No. 249832, November 13, 2024), where the CA downgraded murder to homicide and imposed reclusion temporal, the Court held that the notice of appeal was the wrong remedy but treated it as a Rule 45 petition in the interest of substantial justice. A Rule 45 petition generally raises only questions of law. But because of the constitutional presumption of innocence, the finding of guilt in a criminal case is essentially a question of fact, and an appeal in a criminal case throws the whole case open for review.
alac.application: The CA no longer imposed reclusion perpetua; it imposed a penalty within reclusion temporal. As in Badillo, Pedro's notice of appeal was the wrong mode, but the Court may relax the rule and treat it as a Rule 45 petition. Once the case is before it, the Court may examine the evidence on the elements of the crime and correct errors, whether assigned or not.
alac.conclusion: Pedro used the wrong mode of appeal, but the Court may treat it as a Rule 45 petition and review the whole case, including the facts.

notes: First Division. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), M. Lopez, J. (additional member in lieu of Zalameda, J.) and Marquez, J. concurred; Hernando, J. was on official business. The decision states the general rule on criminal appeals by quoting Rule 124, Section 13(c), which mentions "reclusion perpetua, life imprisonment or a lesser penalty." Yet it held that a notice of appeal was the wrong remedy once the CA imposed reclusion temporal after downgrading the offense. The digest states the holding as the Court applied it. The bar questions do not ask for penalty computation.
